title: Under Armour Unveils Custom Navy Football Uniforms Ahead of 2023 Army-Navy Game
summary: The Army–Navy football game, presented by USAA, an enduring and cherished tradition in American sports, is about to see its 124th match-up. This epic showdown not only symbolizes the fierce rivalry between two of the nation's most esteemed military academies but also serves as a poignant reminder of the camaraderie and shared commitment of these future leaders in uniform. Under Armour, renowned for its innovation in athletic apparel, will once again partner with the Navy football team to outfit the Midshipmen.
body_text: Product With a Purpose With a product that carries a profound purpose, this year's Navy football uniforms will be accessible to fans nationwide—available for purchase on Under Armour's website and through retailers across the country. The tradition of these uniforms extends beyond the football field and resonates with Under Armour's unwavering commitment to supporting the armed forces through the UA Freedom collection, which provides an accrual of proceeds directly to veteran-led organizations like Team Rubicon and the National Military Family Association, among others. What’s more, this season’s UA Navy apparel features high-performance cotton tees and updated fleece offerings that celebrate the Navy's heritage, allowing fans to show their support for the team and wear a piece of history that represents the very essence of the Naval Academy's heritage, tradition and values. The submarine-inspired look of this year’s Navy uniforms holds the promise of pushing the Midshipmen to perform at their full potential and bring home the W. This game is a testament to the dedication and commitment of the young men and women who will one day serve our nation, with Under Armour’s commitment to the U.S. armed forces shining through as well. Don't forget to tune in to CBS on December 9th at 3:00 PM ET when the game takes place at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, MA. It's a celebration of tradition, valor, and the indomitable spirit of our armed forces.

title: Best AI Agent Frameworks of 2026
summary: Compare LangChain, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI, Agno, Haystack, LlamaIndex, and the OpenAI Agent SDK on multi-agent support, languages, license, and hosting.
body_text: TL;DR Framework Multi-agent support Languages & SDKs License Hosting LangChain / LangGraph Graph-based orchestration (LangGraph) Python, JavaScript MIT Self-hosted, cloud Microsoft Agent Framework Native + cross-framework coordination Python, C#, Go MIT Self-hosted, Azure CrewAI Role-based "crews" Python MIT Self-hosted, cloud Agno Native "teams" or step-based workflows Python Apache 2.0 Self-hosted Haystack Coordinator/specialist via ComponentTool Python Apache 2.0 Self-hosted, Haystack Enterprise LlamaIndex Workflows Dedicated multi-agent workflow construct Python, TypeScript MIT Self-hosted OpenAI Agent SDK Handoffs or agents-as-tools Python, TypeScript MIT Self-hosted The best AI agent frameworks give you memory, tools, and modularity out of the box. Agentic AI has moved from fragile prototypes in 2024 to production systems in 2026, and the framework you pick now sets the ceiling for what your agent can do. Even Robinhood is now supporting AI agents straight from the app. Investment apps like this used to make bot trading incredibly difficult. When building AI agents, your framework matters even more than your model choice. You can swap a model with one line of code. To swap AI agent frameworks, you need an entirely new harness. What is an agent framework? An agent framework is the harness around a model: memory, tool calls, orchestration, and everything else that turns a plain LLM into an agent. Every AI agent is really two things, a model and a harness, and the framework is what builds the harness for you. Traditional frameworks (Django, Next.js, Scrapy, Playwright) jumpstart application development and let you skip the boilerplate. Agent frameworks do the same for agents. Why use AI agent frameworks? Frameworks give an agent the tooling, memory, and context management that turn a raw model into something useful. Lee Robinson from Cursor frames it with a Mario analogy. In the meme, we see three different versions of Mario. Small Mario : This represents just a model with no tooling or context. It's baseline usability. A user inputs data. The model reads the input and outputs data. Big Mario : In gaming, big Mario can jump higher. He can take more damage. Models follow this same principle. A model with tooling can execute tasks and handle minor setbacks. Powered-up Mario : In the game, at this point Mario is a world away from his initial state. He can take damage, jump higher, and use fireballs. Agents with context and tooling have similar advantages. With memory, your AI agent can rebuild context and finish tasks regardless context length. What exactly does this have to do with agent frameworks? Imagine getting a power-up with Mario. It's easy enough, right? Now imagine coding him to get bigger. Imagine writing the fireball code by hand every time he powers up. Next, imagine building MCP servers and model tools by hand whenever you build an AI agent. This process is tedious and error prone. AI agent frameworks solve this problem. Instead of rewriting agent tools by hand, you plug them in. You don't build a memory system. Memory and tooling are done with a single import. AI agent frameworks accelerate the build process. They help us build and iterate model harnesses quickly. Instead of building everything from scratch, we get standardized, reusable pieces. With a well-built harness, you can swap your models easily, and your agentic system remains intact. You could even swap models midtask. The new model picks up where the old one left off. Who needs AI agent frameworks? If you're building AI agents, you need frameworks. Even the most basic frameworks save time and effort. Imagine a simple math assistant. There are several architectures you could use. As Perl creator Larry Wall would say, "TIMTOWTDI" (pronounced as "Tim Toady"). It's an acronym for "there is more than one way to do it." Potential setups: Just the model : User asks the model, "What's the answer to 2+2?" The model then uses its training data to predict the answer. For 1+1 and other well-documented problems, this can work. As equations get more complicated, the model is more prone to error. It doesn't follow deterministic rules. The model performs a best guess answer. Often, the best guess just isn't good enough. Coding model : If a model can code, it can solve problems. This model would take the user's equation (1+1), and write a script to calculate the output. In extremely complex situations, this may be required. For simple math, this is overkill. The model doesn't need new tools for every question you ask it. Tool calling : This is the sweet spot. We can write four functions: add() , subtract() , multiply() , and divide() . We can then wrap them as tools. When the model needs to solve an equation, it passes 1+1 into add() . The tool returns the answer, and the AI agent pipes the answer back to the user. What makes an ideal AI agent framework? An ideal agent framework covers four capabilities: interchangeable models and providers, first-class support for MCP and command-line tools, straightforward memory configuration, and a choice between in-RAM and persistent memory. Interchangeable models : Multiple providers need to be supported. You should be able to switch between GPT-5.6 , Fable, or Mythos 5 , and even GLM 5.2 seamlessly. Tool support : Agents need to call existing tools with a standard protocol like MCP or skills and CLI . Users also need to be able to create custom tools easily by wrapping functions for LLM usage. An AI agent should be able to use the Firecrawl API , operate a calculator, and any other tools it needs. Memory : Without memory, sometimes even a single webpage can overwhelm an AI agent's context window. For prototyping and one-offs, your AI agent can use in-RAM memory. For complex tasks, at a minimum, memory should be stored on a local drive or in the cloud. At scale, multi-agent architecture (agent swarms) should support this too. For customer support, you'll likely need multiple agents assisting multiple customers. In a data pipeline, you might use a frontier model to supervise outputs coming from less advanced parsing models. Multi-agent support is essential for any agent framework aimed at production and scale. Three more production concerns matter alongside it. Programming languages : Your SDK needs to match your programming environment. If Python is your daily driver, you shouldn't need to bridge Go or JavaScript code to your Python environment. Licensing : Permissive licensing is just as important. Software licensing can range from highly permissive like MIT or ISC to highly restricted licenses like GPL , which are completely incompatible with proprietary codebases. Hosting : Most frameworks can be self-hosted. With strong DevOps. you can deploy self-hosted instances to the cloud. Some providers help you skip the DevOps work and deploy straight to their cloud. What are the top AI agent frameworks in 2026? Let's go over the top AI agent frameworks of 2026. We'll evaluate each provider using the following criteria. Supported programming languages Licensing Multi-agent support Hosting To be clear, each of these AI agent frameworks supports some form of model interchangeability, tool calling/MCP support, and memory. Since all the frameworks support them, they won't impact ranking. LangChain LangChain set the initial standard for AI agents . Their project started off as a way to write tools for LLMs. It has since evolved into a full stack for agentic programming. LangChain handles agent building and tool calls. LangGraph provides graph-based orchestration to manage agents at scale. LangSmith allows teams to monitor their AI agents and system performance in real time. Multi-agent support: Manage agents at scale with LangGraph. Supported languages and SDKs: Python and JavaScript. License: MIT Hosting: Self-hosted and cloud deployment Microsoft Agent Framework Microsoft Agent Framework is a consolidation of Semantic Kernel and AutoGen . It offers multi-agent orchestration and cross-runtime interoperability, so agents built in Microsoft Agent Framework can coordinate with agents built in entirely separate frameworks. Microsoft Agent Framework inherits things like state management, type safety, middleware, and telemetry from Semantic Kernel. It combines these features with the simple abstractions used in AutoGen as well as graph-based orchestration. Multi-agent support: Supports both native multi-agent orchestration as well as cross-framework coordination. Supported languages and SDKs: Python, C#, Go License: MIT Hosting: Self-hosted and cloud deployments via Azure CrewAI CrewAI was designed for multi-agent swarms. You can assemble a team, or "crew" of AI agents with specific roles. For instance, if I want to develop a mobile app, I could create a backend coding agent, a frontend agent, and a swarm of AI tester agents. On the enterprise tier, AI agents run inside a governance layer with role-based privileges, audit trails, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints. You can learn more about building swarms with CrewAI here . Multi-agent support: Role-based "crews". Supported languages and SDKs: Python License: MIT Hosting: Self-hosted and cloud deployment Agno Agno supports agent creation, bundling session management, memory, knowledge, and human-in-the-loop support into a single runtime called AgentOS. It's built for teams who need granular control over their agentic stack. For multi-agent work, Agno lets you assemble agents into an autonomous, collaborative team. Agno also supports linear, step-based workflows. Multi-agent support: Native "teams" or step-based linear workflows Supported languages and SDKs: Python License: Apache 2.0 Hosting: Self-hosted Haystack Haystack is a Python framework with full agent support, originally built for RAG pipelines and semantic search. Multi-agent architecture is possible in Haystack but implemented at a lower level than in most frameworks. Rather than creating a swarm or crew, you wrap your AI agent using ComponentTool and let a coordinator delegate tasks to other agents. Multi-agent support: Coordinator and specialist pattern using ComponentTool Supported languages and SDKs: Python License: Apache 2.0 Hosting: Self-hosted and cloud options are available through Haystack Enterprise LlamaIndex Workflows LlamaIndex started off as a framework for connecting AI models to documents. It spread into early agentic architectures. As time passed, they expanded to support agent building and built LlamaIndex Workflows . LlamaIndex now includes a dedicated agent construct with support for human-in-the-loop validation. You can create agents with a simple class and then pass a list of agents into an agent workflow. Multi-agent support: Dedicated multi-agent workflow construct Supported languages and SDKs: Python, TypeScript License: MIT Hosting: Self-hosted OpenAI Agent SDK The OpenAI Agent SDK grew out of their experimental Swarm project. Users can wrap functions as tools straight from the SDK. When building agents, pass the tools into the agent constructor. For multi-agent support, developers can use handoffs to pass work between autonomous or semi-autonomous decentralized agents. If you need one agent to manage others, you can use agents-as-tools and pass them directly into another agent. Multi-agent support: Decentralized handoffs or agents-as-tools where a dedicated manager stays in control Supported languages and SDKs: Python, TypeScript License: MIT Hosting: Self-hosted Give your agents web data access with Firecrawl With the Firecrawl API, developers can programmatically use tools for web access. The API currently supports the following features. Search : Run live web searches for structured, accurate results. Scrape : Fetch individual webpages reliably, with robust infrastructure that handles modern websites. Interact : Launch live web browsers and interact with webpages to load content dynamically. Crawl : Crawl entire websites or extract all their links using a single call. Agent : Using natural language, prompt a dedicated AI agent to perform deep research on a topic of your choice. All of the AI agent frameworks listed above support MCP. To configure MCP with them, you can add your configuration. { "mcpServers" : { "firecrawl-mcp" : { "command" : "npx" , "args" : [ "-y" , "firecrawl-mcp" ] , "env" : { "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY" : "<your-firecrawl-api-key>" } } } } Firecrawl now also supports keyless MCP usage . Users are subject to rate limiting and tool restrictions when using the keyless MCP. More details can be found here . Whichever framework you pick, plug Firecrawl in and your agents get web data on day one.

title: Welcoming Phil Nash, our new Developer Experience Engineer
summary: We're thrilled to share the news that Phil Nash is joining Resend.
body_text: Today, we're excited to share that Phil Nash is joining the team as DX Engineer. He spent 8 years at Twilio teaching developers through talks, articles, and live coding. From there, he took that same passion to IBM. At Resend, he'll keep doing what he does best: helping developers be more productive. My favorite talk from Phil is Let's build an AI agent . More about Phil How did you get into software? I remember a school computing class at the age of 13 where I got to build my first HTML page. In a world before CSS, I distinctly recall making the background of the page maroon and adding further style by wrapping everything in a <TABLE> element (everything in HTML was in all caps back then) with a huge, bevelled border to make it seem as though it was sticking out of the page. It was glorious and it kicked off my love affair with the web. I pursued further computing subjects, eventually taking on a degree in maths and computer science. That almost put me off the world of software: Java and I did not agree. However, while I was supposed to be studying for my final exams, I instead found myself building websites. Once I was finished with university, I built myself a WordPress blog and started learning and writing about front-end development. That eventually led to my first job in the industry and the start of my career in software. What does your desktop/home screen look like? Phil's desktop, no clutter yet Why are you at Resend? I've followed Zeno Rocha for quite a while now so when I saw he'd started Resend I knew I'd have to keep an eye on it. I used Resend to build a contact form on my own personal site , and even wrote my own simple TypeScript client to interact with the API (don't use it, the official client is much better!). Sending email is such a fundamental part of almost every application out there, so when the opportunity arose to join the team and help make that the best possible experience for developers, I had to go for it. Where do you find #inspiration? I find inspiration in my friends and developers in the industry that I look up to. This is why you find me on social networks that show you the people you follow, not what the algorithm thinks you should see. That way I get to experience the creativity and passion of people I believe in. It's why I love going to meetups and conferences, where I can watch people present about topics they are passionate about. It's why I wanted to join Resend and work alongside people who care about the work that they do. I find inspiration in other people's passion. If you weren't programming, what would you be doing? In a past life, I played bass in a band that got some radio airplay in the UK, but fizzled out before really achieving anything. Before that, I once played rugby union for the Harlequins under-19 team, so there's the tiniest chance I could have made it in professional sports. In reality, I was too small for top-flight rugby and far from talented enough to be a real musician, but either would have made for fun careers. Favorite tool? Part of why I'm a web developer is that the browser is my favourite tool. It's a canvas on which to build, a portal to the whole web, and a scripting environment just waiting for you in dev tools. The list of things you can't do in or with a browser is already short, but the browser developers keep chipping away at it. Firefox has been my daily driver for more than 20 years now, but Chrome is always the second thing I download on a new machine. Favorite hotkey? As I have been setting up my laptop, it has dawned on me that I am not a hardcore developer who needs to have his hands on the keyboard at all times. I cannot live without mouse gestures. Gesturefy is the add-on that helps me whip about the web in a carefree manner that I just can't manage without it installed. If I had to pick a hotkey though, powering up Raycast with Cmd + Space is my top choice. Favorite place to visit? I love visiting Spain, and have always liked Barcelona. The combination of the sea, the food, the architecture, and the vibe has always made me happy. Though last year I visited San Sebastián for the first time and it made a strong claim. Phil and Kelly with San Sebastián laid out behind them Advice for ambitious software engineers? Since starting up that WordPress blog when I was trying to get my career going, the thing that has worked for me over and over again is to share what I have learned. So I recommend that every time you learn something new, you write it down, turn it into a presentation, make a video, or otherwise share it with the developer community somehow. This has several benefits: In order to explain something to someone else, you will need to dig deeper into the topic and you will understand it better Sharing your learning publicly can help others to understand the topic too The worst-case scenario is that you have documented something for yourself in the future that you can refer back to But often that worst-case doesn't happen and instead you end up building a community around you of people you can teach, learn from, and be inspired by. And in the best-case you land yourself a job at a fantastic company like Resend.

title: Introducing the Iterative Mapping Grant Program
summary: Run 12 samples on the Nautilus Voyager™ Platform at no charge.
body_text: Tau proteoforms may hold the key to understanding neurodegenerative disease progress, but until now, no platform could quantify them at scale. The Iterative Mapping Grant Program provides researchers with free access to the Nautilus Tau Proteoforms Assay. The assay quantifies up to 768 full-length tau proteoforms at the single-molecule level on the Nautilus Voyager™ Platform. Through the Iterative Mapping Grant program, 3 researchers will be selected to join the Iterative Mapping Early Access Program at no charge. Each will receive analysis of 12 samples, experimental design support from Nautilus scientists, a final data report built for easy interpretation, help presenting results at a mutually agreed-upon conference, and assistance preparing a peer-reviewed publication. We provide brief details on the program below and encourage you to visit the program webpage for more information as well as the program’s full terms and conditions . Download the Iterative Mapping Early Access Program Brochure for more information on the Nautilus Tau Proteoforms Assay. How to apply to the Iterative Mapping Grant Program To apply, submit a proposal for a 12-sample project on the grant program webpage by July 31, 2026, with samples ready to ship by November 30, 2026. Applicants must also be willing to be publicly announced as grant recipients and to let Nautilus reference their work in future marketing materials. Sample sources and types must match the specifications listed on the grant program webpage, so be sure to check there before submitting. Iterative Mapping Grant Program project ideas Not sure what to propose? Find some brief ideas that might make good seeds for grants below. We have a few additional ideas on the grant program website and encourage you to reach out to marketing@nautlus.bio if you have any questions about potential projects. Differentiating tauopathies by their distinct tau proteoform profiles . This could sharpen diagnostic tools across diseases. Identifying which tau proteoforms are most likely to seed aggregation or spread between neurons . Identifying these proteoforms may be central to understanding disease progression. Exploring which tau proteoforms are associated with known disease risk variants. Such explorations may reveal the mechanistic links between genetic risk and disease development. Visit the Iterative Mapping Grant Program webpage for more information as well as the program’s full terms and conditions . Winners will be announced on or before August 14, 2026. Good luck! title: Travis Russell joins German American Bank as Regional President
body_text: German American Bank announces Bowling Green native, Travis Russell, has joined the company as Regional President. In this role, he will lead the Company’s financial team serving Warren, Simpson, Barren, and Hart Counties in South Central Kentucky in delivering relationship-focused commercial and personal banking and wealth management services. Travis joins the local leadership team of Kim Thomas, Senior Vice President of Retail Banking, and Todd Kanipe, Regional Credit Officer. “Travis brings a tremendous amount of talent to an already strong and dedicated team of professionals in Bowling Green, Glasgow, Franklin, Horse Cave, and Munfordville,” states Neil Dauby, German American Bank Chairman and CEO. “His experience as a community leader makes him a great fit for German American Bank and our focus on local decision making, relationship-building, and strong community involvement. I look forward to watching the leadership team of Travis, Kim and Todd grow our presence in the South Central Kentucky area.” Russell brings over 10 years of commercial banking experience to this role, holding various positions at American Bank and Trust and J.P. Morgan Chase Bank in the Bowling Green area. He is a graduate of Western Kentucky University with a degree in Finance and obtained an MBA from the University of Kentucky. As a lifelong Bowling Green resident, Travis has deep rooted connections and presence in his community. He is currently a member of the Cornerstone Committee for LifeWorks, and is a graduate of Leadership Bowling Green and the Kentucky Bankers Association Emerging Leader Program. He has also served as a Board member and President of the Bowling Green Country Club. Travis and his wife Alyssa live in Bowling Green with their son, Chapman, and daughter, Elsie Blair. "I’ve always been impressed with German American Bank’s reputation for community involvement. The company’s strength and stability speak for its historical successes. I am joining a seasoned and strong team of commercial and personal bankers and I am thrilled be a part of our continued success and growth in our local communities," said Russell. Share Copy Email

title: Métricas de talento humano: cómo conectar datos de personas con resultados del negocio
summary: Conecta datos de talento con resultados de negocio. Elige métricas clave, dales contexto y decide con precisión.
body_text: Medir talento humano no debería servir únicamente para llenar reportes internos. Si las métricas no ayudan a entender qué está pasando con las personas, qué capacidades necesita la empresa y qué decisiones debe tomar RRHH, terminan siendo datos acumulados sin impacto real. ‍ El problema no suele ser la falta de información. Muchas organizaciones ya tienen datos de capacitación, clima, desempeño, rotación o evaluaciones. El reto está en conectarlos para entender cómo influyen en los resultados del negocio. ‍ Por eso, hablar de métricas de talento humano implica mirar más allá de indicadores aislados. Una empresa necesita saber qué competencias tiene, qué brechas limitan el desempeño, qué equipos requieren desarrollo, qué señales anticipan rotación y qué tan alineado está el talento con las prioridades estratégicas. ‍ Medir talento para mejorar resultados, no solo para reportar ‍ Un área de RRHH puede saber cuántas personas fueron capacitadas, cuántas evaluaciones se aplicaron o cuántos colaboradores salieron durante el año. Esa información es útil, pero no siempre explica qué debe hacerse después. ‍ La diferencia aparece cuando las métricas responden preguntas de negocio: ‍ ¿Qué competencias están frenando el desempeño? ¿Qué programas de capacitación generan avance real? ¿Qué equipos muestran señales de desgaste? ¿Qué áreas tienen mayor riesgo de rotación? ¿Qué perfiles necesitan desarrollo prioritario? ¿Qué relación existe entre clima, aprendizaje y resultados? ‍ Medir talento con intención permite que RRHH deje de reportar solo actividad y empiece a mostrar cómo las personas influyen en productividad, retención, crecimiento y ejecución. ‍ Qué son las métricas de talento humano ‍ Las métricas de talento humano son datos que permiten evaluar procesos, comportamientos, capacidades y resultados relacionados con las personas dentro de una organización. ‍ Pueden medir actividades operativas, avances de desarrollo, brechas, desempeño, compromiso o impacto en resultados de negocio. ‍ No todas las métricas tienen el mismo valor. Algunas ayudan a administrar procesos. Otras permiten tomar decisiones estratégicas. ‍ Datos operativos ‍ Los datos operativos muestran actividad y cumplimiento. ‍ Ejemplos: ‍ número de colaboradores capacitados evaluaciones completadas vacantes cubiertas cursos finalizados asistencia a programas encuestas respondidas ‍ Estos datos son necesarios porque permiten saber si los procesos se ejecutan. Pero por sí solos no siempre muestran impacto. ‍ Saber que 300 personas completaron un curso no explica si aprendieron, aplicaron algo nuevo o mejoraron su desempeño. ‍ Datos estratégicos ‍ Los datos estratégicos ayudan a entender cómo las personas contribuyen al negocio. ‍ Ejemplos: ‍ brechas de competencias por área desempeño de equipos críticos rotación de talento clave clima por líder avance de planes de desarrollo movilidad interna relación entre capacitación y resultados ‍ Estos datos permiten hacer preguntas más útiles. No solo muestran qué ocurrió, sino qué podría estar afectando la operación. ‍ Indicadores de impacto ‍ Los indicadores de impacto conectan talento con resultados. ‍ Por ejemplo, una empresa puede analizar si una ruta de capacitación redujo errores operativos, si una evaluación de competencias permitió mejorar desempeño o si un programa de liderazgo ayudó a disminuir rotación en mandos medios. ‍ 1. Operativa Muestra la actividad realizada . Ayuda a responder: ¿Se ejecutó el proceso? ‍ 2. Estratégica Muestra el estado del talento . Ayuda a responder: ¿Dónde hay brechas o riesgos? ‍ 3. Impacto Muestra la relación con resultados . Ayuda a responder: ¿Qué cambió después de actuar? ‍ El objetivo no es eliminar las métricas operativas. Es complementarlas con datos que ayuden a decidir. ‍ Métricas clave de talento humano ‍ Las métricas más útiles dependen del objetivo de la empresa. No todas las organizaciones necesitan medir lo mismo con la misma prioridad. ‍ Sin embargo, hay cinco dimensiones que suelen ofrecer una visión más completa del talento: competencias, capacitación, desempeño, compromiso y rotación. ‍ Brechas de competencias ‍ Las brechas de competencias muestran la distancia entre las capacidades actuales de los colaboradores y las capacidades que necesita la organización. ‍ Esta métrica ayuda a identificar dónde hace falta desarrollar talento antes de que el problema impacte en resultados. ‍ Por ejemplo: ‍ brechas de liderazgo pueden afectar clima y retención brechas digitales pueden limitar productividad brechas técnicas pueden generar errores de calidad brechas de comunicación pueden provocar retrabajo brechas comerciales pueden afectar ventas ‍ Cuando RRHH mide desarrollo de competencias laborales con claridad, puede priorizar rutas, planes y acciones de desarrollo según las necesidades reales del negocio. ‍ Avance de capacitación ‍ El avance de capacitación permite entender si los colaboradores están progresando en sus programas de aprendizaje. ‍ Pero esta métrica debe ir más allá de finalización. Un buen análisis debería observar: ‍ avance por ruta finalización por equipo participación por rol contenidos pendientes evaluación de aprendizaje aplicación posterior relación con brechas detectadas ‍ En capacitación, los indicadores de capacitación aportan más valor cuando ayudan a entender si el aprendizaje se está aplicando y no solo si las personas completaron cursos. ‍ Desempeño ‍ Las métricas de desempeño muestran cómo contribuyen las personas a los objetivos de la organización. ‍ Pueden incluir cumplimiento de metas, evaluaciones, feedback, resultados por equipo o desempeño por rol. ‍ Algunas métricas útiles son: ‍ cumplimiento de objetivos individuales desempeño por equipo evolución del desempeño por periodo frecuencia de feedback planes de mejora activos relación entre desempeño y competencias ‍ El desempeño no debería analizarse solo para calificar. También debe servir para entender qué necesita cada persona o equipo para mejorar. ‍ Compromiso ‍ El compromiso ayuda a entender qué tan conectadas están las personas con la empresa, su equipo y su trabajo. ‍ Puede medirse mediante encuestas, eNPS, participación, permanencia, feedback cualitativo o señales de involucramiento en programas internos. ‍ Algunas señales de bajo compromiso pueden aparecer antes de una renuncia: ‍ baja participación en capacitación menor interacción con líderes poca respuesta a encuestas caída en desempeño comentarios negativos recurrentes desinterés en oportunidades de desarrollo ‍ El compromiso no debe verse como una percepción aislada. Conviene cruzarlo con clima, liderazgo, aprendizaje y crecimiento. ‍ Rotación ‍ La rotación es una de las métricas más visibles, pero también una de las más incompletas si se analiza sola. ‍ No basta con saber cuántas personas salen. Es necesario entender quiénes salen, cuándo, de qué áreas, con qué antigüedad y después de qué experiencias. ‍ Algunas métricas útiles son: ‍ rotación voluntaria rotación involuntaria rotación temprana rotación de talento clave permanencia promedio salidas por área salidas por líder relación entre rotación y clima ‍ La rotación puede ser un síntoma de problemas más profundos: falta de desarrollo, liderazgo débil, mal onboarding, baja claridad del rol o poca posibilidad de crecimiento. ‍ Ejemplos de métricas accionables ‍ Una métrica accionable no solo muestra un dato. Ayuda a decidir qué hacer. ‍ 1. Alta rotación en nuevos ingresos Métrica relevante: rotación durante primeros 90 días . Acción posible: ajustar onboarding . ‍ 2. Bajo desempeño en un equipo Métrica relevante: brechas de competencias + resultados . Acción posible: crear ruta de desarrollo . ‍ 3. Baja participación en cursos Métrica relevante: avance de capacitación por área . Acción posible: revisar relevancia y seguimiento . ‍ 4. Clima bajo con alta carga Métrica relevante: clima + ausentismo + rotación . Acción posible: revisar liderazgo y prioridades . ‍ 5. Talento clave sin crecimiento Métrica relevante: movilidad interna + planes de desarrollo . Acción posible: activar conversaciones de carrera . ‍ 6. Brechas digitales recurrentes Métrica relevante: evaluación de competencias + avance de rutas . Acción posible: priorizar capacitación digital . ‍ Este tipo de lectura permite pasar de datos descriptivos a decisiones concretas. ‍ Errores comunes al medir talento humano ‍ Muchas empresas tienen datos, pero no siempre tienen una lectura útil del talento. El problema suele estar en cómo se interpretan y conectan esas métricas. ‍ No conectar métricas ‍ El error más frecuente es analizar cada dato por separado. ‍ Capacitación por un lado. Clima por otro. Desempeño en otro archivo. Rotación en otro reporte. ‍ Cuando las métricas viven separadas, RRHH puede tardar demasiado en detectar patrones. ‍ Por ejemplo: ‍ Un área tiene baja participación en aprendizaje. Sus brechas de competencias siguen abiertas. El desempeño empieza a caer. La rotación aumenta meses después. ‍ Si esos datos se hubieran conectado antes, la empresa habría tenido señales más tempranas para intervenir. ‍ No segmentar por área ‍ Los promedios generales pueden ocultar problemas importantes. ‍ Una empresa puede tener buena participación general en capacitación, pero bajo avance en mandos medios. Puede tener clima aceptable a nivel organización, pero un área con señales de desgaste. Puede tener rotación controlada, pero perder talento clave en roles críticos. ‍ Por eso, las métricas de talento humano deben segmentarse por: ‍ área rol nivel sede antigüedad líder competencia etapa del ciclo laboral ‍ Sin segmentación, las decisiones se vuelven demasiado generales. ‍ No interpretar causas ‍ Una métrica muestra una señal, pero no siempre muestra la causa. ‍ Si la rotación sube, la solución no siempre es mejorar beneficios. Si la capacitación tiene bajo avance, el problema no siempre es falta de interés. Si el clima baja, no siempre se resuelve con una iniciativa de bienestar. ‍ La interpretación requiere cruzar datos y formular hipótesis. ‍ 1. Baja capacitación Posible causa: contenido poco relevante . Dato adicional que conviene revisar: brechas, rol y feedback de líderes . ‍ 2. Alta rotación Posible causa: falta de crecimiento . Dato adicional que conviene revisar: planes de desarrollo, clima y desempeño . ‍ 3. Bajo desempeño Posible causa: brecha técnica o de liderazgo . Dato adicional que conviene revisar: competencias, feedback y objetivos . ‍ 4. Clima bajo Posible causa: carga o mala comunicación . Dato adicional que conviene revisar: área, líder, rotación y ausentismo . ‍ 5. Bajo compromiso Posible causa: poca conexión con futuro . Dato adicional que conviene revisar: movilidad, aprendizaje y reconocimiento . ‍ La métrica es el punto de partida. La decisión viene después del análisis. ‍ Checklist para evaluar si tus métricas de talento son útiles ‍ Antes de sumar más indicadores, conviene revisar si los datos actuales realmente ayudan a tomar decisiones. ‍ ¿Las métricas responden a objetivos de negocio? ¿Se conectan datos de aprendizaje, desempeño, clima y rotación? ¿Existe segmentación por área, rol o nivel? ¿RRHH puede detectar brechas de competencias? ¿Los indicadores muestran evolución, no solo actividad? ¿Los líderes reciben información accionable? ¿Las métricas ayudan a priorizar planes de desarrollo? ¿Se revisa si las acciones tomadas mejoran los resultados? ¿La empresa puede anticipar riesgos antes de que escalen? ‍ Si varias respuestas son negativas, probablemente la empresa tiene reportes, pero todavía no tiene una visión integral del talento. ‍ Cómo Lapzo conecta datos de talento ‍ Para que las métricas de talento humano ayuden a tomar mejores decisiones, la empresa necesita centralizar información clave y verla como parte de un mismo sistema. ‍ Lapzo permite conectar datos de competencias, aprendizaje, evaluaciones y objetivos para que RRHH tenga una visión más clara del desarrollo de talento. ‍ Competencias ‍ Lapzo permite trabajar desde competencias, identificando brechas por persona, rol o equipo. ‍ Esto ayuda a que RRHH entienda qué capacidades necesitan desarrollarse y qué rutas pueden cerrar esas brechas con mayor precisión. ‍ Aprendizaje ‍ Los datos de aprendizaje permiten visualizar avance, participación y cumplimiento de rutas. ‍ Con esta información, RRHH puede saber qué personas avanzan, qué contenidos funcionan y qué equipos requieren seguimiento adicional. ‍ Evaluaciones ‍ Las evaluaciones ayudan a conectar desempeño, competencias y necesidades de desarrollo. ‍ En lugar de evaluar solo para calificar, la empresa puede usar esos datos para construir planes más claros. ‍ Objetivos ‍ Conectar métricas de talento con objetivos permite entender cómo el desarrollo impacta en prioridades del negocio. ‍ Cuando aprendizaje, competencias y desempeño se observan juntos, RRHH puede tomar decisiones más precisas sobre qué desarrollar, dónde intervenir y cómo medir avance. ‍ Conclusión ‍ Las métricas de talento humano son útiles cuando ayudan a entender cómo las personas impactan en los resultados del negocio. ‍ Para lograrlo, RRHH necesita ir más allá de reportes aislados y conectar datos de aprendizaje, competencias, desempeño, clima y rotación. Solo así puede detectar patrones, anticipar riesgos y diseñar acciones más efectivas. ‍ Medir talento no se trata de tener más indicadores. Se trata de elegir los datos correctos, interpretarlos con contexto y convertirlos en decisiones. ‍ Con Lapzo, las organizaciones pueden centralizar información de talento, visualizar brechas, dar seguimiento al aprendizaje y conectar evaluaciones con objetivos para mejorar la toma de decisiones. ‍

title: Legora enters Latin America with a new Mexico City office
summary: Legora, the agentic operating system for legal professionals trusted by more than 100,000 lawyers at more than 1,500 leading law firms and in-house legal teams across over 50 markets, today announced the opening of an office in Mexico City – its first in Latin America.
body_text: The office establishes Legora's presence in a market where cross-border investment, evolving North American trade rules, and rapid legal AI adoption are converging to reshape how legal work gets done. The region's appetite for legal AI backs that up. Latin America's legal tech market is on track to nearly triple by 2033. Adoption is still early relative to Europe and the US, but the direction of travel, and the pace of it, is what drew Legora to establish a base there. Legora is already working with several customers in the region. "Latin America's legal market is at an inflection point," said Max Junestrand, CEO and Co-Founder of Legora. "Nearshoring and broader shifts in regional trade are driving increasingly complex cross-border legal work while AI adoption among legal professionals across the region is accelerating. We want to be on the ground to support that transition.” The Legora office will open with a local team focused on customer success, legal engineering and go to market. Being on the ground matters to how Legora works with customers: the company builds its platform in close collaboration with the firms and legal teams that use it. "The firms getting the most out of Legora are the ones we're sitting next to in their offices, in their workflows, hearing directly what's working and what isn't," said Patrick Forquer, CRO of Legora. “We're excited to keep building this together with our customers there, just closer than before." The expansion into Latin America caps twelve months of rapid growth for Legora. Over the past year, the company raised a $600 million Series D at a $5.6 billion valuation, surpassing $100 million in annual recurring revenue. Its customer base has grown from several hundred law firms and in-house teams to more than 1,500 across over 50 markets, and its footprint has expanded from a handful of hubs to 17 offices spanning Europe, North America, Asia-Pacific, and now Latin America.
